solution: Mark the cups 1, k+1, 2k+1, ... up to index n; there are m = ceil(n/k) of them and, because they are spaced exactly k apart, every window of k consecutive cups contains exactly one marked cup, so pouring only into marked cups turns the problem into the abstract game: distribute at most x litres among m slots, then the opponent zeroes one slot of its choice. That abstraction is also an upper bound on any strategy, because the opponent can restrict itself to the m windows covering the disjoint blocks of k cups (clipping the last window to end at cup n, which only destroys more), and then the maximum inside a block behaves exactly like a single slot. In the m-slot game the optimum is x times one plus the harmonic number of m-1: if u slots are still alive at a common level v, pouring x/u into each and losing one keeps the quantity v plus x times the harmonic number of u invariant, and the last surviving slot is topped up by the final free pour. The published solution realises exactly that: about 1900 rounds level all m marked cups towards x (refilling whichever was just drained and splitting the remaining x equally makes the common level approach x geometrically at rate 1-1/m), then at most 99 rounds pour x/u into the u slots the opponent has not yet drained, shrinking u to one, and the final pour adds x. It sends at most 1999 POUR lines, exactly x litres per round, and runs in O(rounds * m) time and O(m) space.

solution_source.used: The problem is interactive, so I wrote a full interactor (verify_milkteabattle.py) that enforces every judge rule -- distinct in-range cup indices, each amount in [0,x], per-round total at most (1+1e-6)x, strictly fewer than 2000 POUR lines -- and played the compiled binary against six opponents over 400+ games covering the whole constraint box. Against all four minimising opponents the final maximum equals x*(1+H_{m-1}) to nine decimals in every single game, which confirms both the solution and the value of OPT; the value x*(1+H_2) = 2.5x for m = 3 was independently confirmed by value iteration on the continuous three-slot game (2.400, 2.450, 2.475, 2.48750 at grid steps 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125, i.e. exactly 2.5 minus the step).

statement_summary: In an interactive, adaptive game with at most fifty cups, one player repeatedly distributes at most a fixed number of litres of milk tea among cups, after which opponents empty a window of consecutive cups of a fixed length, at most ten. He may instead end with a last distribution nobody drinks, and within two thousand rounds must guarantee some cup holds essentially the largest amount any strategy can force.
notes: game-theory passes the corpus trap: the opponent genuinely chooses which window to drink and the interactor is explicitly adaptive, so the answer is a minimax value, not a simulation. Deliberately NOT labelled game-dp or grundy-numbers (the game is continuous and has no position DP or Sprague-Grundy decomposition), greedy (the even split is forced by an invariant, and calling it greedy hides why 1 + H_{m-1} is optimal), binary-search-answer (nothing is searched for), and probability-dp / expected-value-dp (no randomness anywhere). Vocabulary gap: the corpus has no slug for adversarial/minimax strategy design, nor for the potential-function argument that fixes the value; interactive plus game-theory is the closest pair. FINDING about the published solution, recorded because a reviewer should know: it is optimal against any opponent that plays to minimise, but it is not robust against a wasteful one. It burns 1900 of its 1999 POUR rounds on the levelling phase and leaves only 99 for the knock-out phase, and the knock-out phase only makes progress when the opponent drinks a window it has not already emptied. My interactor that always drinks the leftmost window leaves it at 0.73 to 0.77 of OPT for k = 1 and n >= 47 (it also then finishes with sl-d = 46 slots still alive, which the code silently accepts). The five failures are all against that deliberately wasteful opponent; the four minimising opponents, including one restricted to whole blocks and one that never repeats a window, all give exactly OPT. A judge interactor that plays to minimise -- which is what an adaptive jury does here -- never triggers this, which is consistent with the source being accepted, but the margin is zero: the solution lands exactly on OPT and never above it.
